title: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
summary: Serve hundreds of fine-tunes from one base model: why per-model serving wastes GPUs, merge vs unmerged, Punica's SGMV kernel, S-LoRA's unified paging, vLLM and LoRAX knobs, and the memory and bandwidth costs.
outcomes: Explain why separate per-fine-tune deployments waste both memory and decode batching
Choose between merged, merge-and-swap and unmerged adapter serving for a given traffic mix
Explain how SGMV batches rows for different adapters and why distinct adapters cost bandwidth
Compute adapter memory and its KV-cache equivalent, and explain S-LoRA's unified paging
Configure max_loras, max_lora_rank and max_cpu_loras in vLLM and predict their memory cost

lessons.title: Why serving one model per fine-tune wastes GPUs

blocks.md: Picture a platform where 100 customers each fine-tuned the same 7B base model with LoRA (all linear layers, rank 16, as in the LoRA course). Every customer wants an endpoint. The obvious plan is to merge each adapter into the base weights and deploy 100 independent models. The Punica paper describes the cost: if one model needs $k$ GPUs, $n$ fine-tunes served this way need $k \times n$ GPUs, ignoring that they all share 99% of their weights.

Memory makes this concrete. With Llama-2-7B's shape (6.74B parameters, 16-bit), one merged copy is 13.5 GB, so 100 copies are 1.35 TB. The adapters themselves are tiny: rank 16 on all seven linear layers of 32 layers is 40.0M parameters, 80 MB in 16-bit. One base plus 100 adapters is 21.5 GB.

blocks.title: Weight memory for 100 fine-tunes of a 7B model

scenes.caption: Merging every adapter duplicates the 13.5 GB base 100 times: 1,348 GB of weights before any KV cache.
Keeping adapters separate stores the base once: 13.5 GB + 100 x 80 MB = 21.5 GB. Even 1,000 adapters (93.5 GB) take about as much as 7 merged copies (94 GB).

blocks.md: Memory is only half the waste. Recall from the inference course that each **decode step** reads all the weights to produce one token per sequence, so it is limited by memory bandwidth, not arithmetic. Batching many sequences into one step shares that weight read. Punica's measurements (Figure 1) show that going from batch 1 to batch 32 raised the decode step from 11 ms to 13 ms for short sequences (17 ms to 34 ms for long ones). Thirty-two times the tokens for a small fraction more time.

Separate models split the traffic. If 100 endpoints each see a trickle of requests, each one decodes at batch size 1 to 3 and pays nearly the full weight read per token. Punica reports exactly this for baseline systems: with each request on a distinct LoRA model they ran at batch size 1, and with mixed popularity mostly at batch sizes of 1 to 3.

scenes.caption: One model per fine-tune: three full copies, each decoding its own tiny batch, each paying the full weight read per step.
Shared base: all requests join one batch over a single copy of the base weights, and each request adds its own small LoRA term. This is multi-LoRA serving.

blocks.md: LoRA fine-tunes share a frozen base. A server that keeps the base once and batches requests for different adapters together gets both the memory saving and the batching efficiency that separate deployments throw away.

blocks.question: 100 merged 7B fine-tunes would fit on a large cluster. Why is serving them as separate models still inefficient when each gets little traffic?
options: Merged models are slower per token than the base model
Each model decodes tiny batches, so most of each weight read serves only one or two tokens
Merged weights cannot use the KV cache
The adapters must be recomputed for every token
blocks.explain: Decode is bandwidth bound: the cost of a step is dominated by reading the weights, and batching shares that read. Splitting traffic across 100 copies leaves each with batch sizes near 1, so GPU time per token stays high.

blocks.question: You host 50 rank-16 all-linear adapters (80 MB each, 16-bit) for one 7B base. How much memory do the adapters take, compared with the base?
options: About 4 GB, under a third of the 13.5 GB base
About 40 GB, three times the base
About 400 MB, negligible
About 675 GB, the same as 50 merged copies
blocks.explain: 50 x 80 MB = 4.0 GB. That is real memory, which matters later when adapters compete with the KV cache, but it is small next to 50 x 13.5 GB = 675 GB for merged copies.

lessons.title: Merge, swap, or compute the adapter on the fly

blocks.md: With one base in memory there are two ways to apply adapters. **Merge and swap**: the LoRA paper's suggestion is to fold an adapter into the base, $W = W_0 + BA$, serve it, and to switch tasks subtract $BA$ and add $B'A'$. **Unmerged**: keep $W_0$ untouched and compute each request's adapter term on the fly, which S-LoRA writes as:

blocks.caption: S-LoRA Eq. 2 (their A is h by r and B is r by d, the transpose of the LoRA paper's naming). The xW part is shared by every request; xAB is per request.

blocks.md: Merging is free per token but serves one adapter at a time, because a merged weight bakes one adapter into every row of the batch. A batch that mixes requests for adapters A, B and C needs each row multiplied by a different weight, which only the unmerged form allows. With a batch $X$ whose row $i$ uses adapter $a(i)$:

blocks.tex: Y = X W_0 + \begin{bmatrix} x_1 A_{a(1)} B_{a(1)} \\ x_2 A_{a(2)} B_{a(2)} \\ \vdots \end{bmatrix}
blocks.caption: One big matmul for the base, plus a different small low-rank product per row.

blocks.md: The extra cost is small in arithmetic. Per token, a rank-16 adapter on a 4096 by 4096 projection costs $16 \times (4096 + 4096)$ multiply-adds against $4096^2$ for the base: 0.78%. S-LoRA's argument is that this overhead is far smaller than what batching the base matmul across all adapters saves.

blocks.title: Toy schedule: 3 adapters, each with 1 request of 4 tokens

scenes.caption: Merge and swap serves adapters one after another. Assumed costs: 12 ms per decode step, 10 ms to unmerge one adapter and merge the next.
Unmerged: A, B and C decode in the same batch. Each step costs a little more (assumed 14 ms with three LoRA add-ons), but all three finish at 56 ms and nobody waits for a swap.

Simplified: real step times depend on batch size, sequence length and kernels. The shape of the result is what S-LoRA measured: merging wins with one adapter, and its throughput declines once more than two adapters are active.

blocks.prompt: S-LoRA compared its unmerged design with a merge-based variant (merge the current adapter before each batch, switch when too many requests wait). With exactly one adapter, which design gives higher throughput?
blocks.reveal: **The merged variant.** S-LoRA's ablation (Figure 9) shows merging wins with one adapter, because it pays the merge once and then runs with no LoRA computation at all. Its throughput declines once there are more than 2 adapters, because switching leaves the GPU underused. The right choice depends on how many adapters are active at once.

blocks.md: Unmerged does not mean easy. Requests in one batch use adapters with different ranks and different sequence lengths, so padding everything into one batched matmul wastes work. S-LoRA's variant that copies adapters into contiguous memory and uses padded batched matmul (S-LoRA-bmm) was much slower than the version with custom kernels.

Merge when one adapter dominates the traffic and per-token latency matters most. Keep adapters unmerged when many adapters are active concurrently, so the base matmul can be batched across all of them.

blocks.question: Why can a merged LoRA model not serve requests for two different adapters in the same batch?
options: Because merged weights are stored in a different data type
Because merging removes the KV cache
Because the batch would need a different weight matrix for different rows, and a merged model has only one
Because the base model must be reloaded from disk for each adapter
blocks.explain: A matmul applies one weight matrix to every row of the batch. After merging, that matrix contains one specific adapter. Mixing adapters in a batch requires the shared W0 plus a per-row low-rank term, which is exactly the unmerged form.

blocks.question: A support-bot product uses a single LoRA fine-tune and is judged on per-token latency. What should it do?
options: Run an unmerged multi-LoRA server with max_loras set high
Swap the adapter in and out every batch
Serve the base model without the adapter
Merge the adapter into the base weights and serve that model
blocks.explain: With one adapter there is nothing to batch across, so the unmerged add-on is pure overhead. Merging gives the base model's cost per token, which is also what S-LoRA's single-adapter ablation found.

lessons.title: Batching different adapters: Punica's SGMV kernel

blocks.md: Punica (Chen et al. 2023) made the unmerged form fast with one CUDA kernel, **Segmented Gather Matrix-Vector multiplication (SGMV)**. The trick starts with ordering: sort the requests in a batch so that all rows using the same adapter sit next to each other. A list of segment boundaries $s$ then says which rows belong to which adapter.

blocks.title: Grouping a decode batch of 8 requests by adapter

scenes.caption: Requests arrive for four different adapters in arbitrary order. A plain batched matmul cannot handle this: each row needs different LoRA weights.
Reorder the batch so equal adapters are contiguous: A A A B B C D D. The base matmul does not care about row order.
Segment starts s = [0, 3, 5, 6, 8]: rows 0 to 2 use adapter A, 3 to 4 use B, 5 uses C, 6 to 7 use D. The kernel reads each adapter's weights once per segment.

blocks.md: Punica's semantics fit in one line: `Y[s[i]:s[i+1]] += X[s[i]:s[i+1]] @ W[i]`. A LoRA layer calls it twice. **SGMV-shrink** multiplies the hidden-size input by each segment's A, producing an r-dimensional vector per row. **SGMV-expand** multiplies that by each segment's B and adds the result into the base output in place.

blocks.title: A reference version of the two SGMV calls

scenes.caption: The base projection runs once for all 8 rows as an ordinary GEMM. This is the expensive part, and it is fully shared.
Shrink: segment 0 (rows 0 to 2) multiplies by adapter A's 4096 x 16 matrix, giving three 16-dim vectors.
The loop covers every segment. A real kernel does not loop on the host: it launches all segments at once, one group of thread blocks per segment.
Expand: each segment's 16-dim vectors are multiplied by that adapter's 16 x 4096 B and added into y in place.
scenes.output: 8 rows done: 1 base GEMM + 2 SGMV launches

blocks.md: How much does mixing adapters cost? Punica's roofline analysis counts work and memory traffic for one SGMV call with $s_n$ rows, $n$ distinct adapters and a weight of shape $h_i \times h_o$:

blocks.tex: \text{FLOP} = 2\, s_n h_i h_o \qquad \text{I/O bytes} = 2\,\big[\, s_n (h_i + h_o) + n\, h_i h_o \big]
blocks.caption: Punica Section 7.1. The factor 2 in I/O is 2 bytes per 16-bit value. Reading adapter weights grows with the number of distinct adapters n.

blocks.md: Plug in Punica's case study, $h_i = 16$, $h_o = 4096$, 64 rows. If all 64 rows share one adapter, the call does 12.8 FLOP per byte. If all 64 use different adapters, it does 0.94 FLOP per byte, the same as a single row: it becomes a pure memory read, which Punica handles with a bandwidth-oriented schedule instead of Tensor Cores.

blocks.title: Measured SGMV latency, batch 1 vs 64 (Punica Figure 8)

scenes.caption: One adapter for every row: 37 microseconds at batch 1 and 40 at batch 64. Batching is nearly free.

Skewed popularity reaches 46 microseconds at batch 64. Every row on its own adapter reaches 116 microseconds, because each row reads its own weights. A step makes many such calls, yet Punica's layer benchmark barely changes with the adapter mix.

blocks.md: At the model level the add-on barely matters. Punica reports 1,044 tokens/s for a 7B model whatever the adapter mix, and for a 70B model 441 to 446 tokens/s, while a vLLM baseline without multi-LoRA support reached about 21 to 25 tokens/s with many adapters (457 tokens/s when serving the backbone alone).

blocks.title: Extra weight bytes read per decode step (simplified)

y.label: adapter bytes as % of base weights

scenes.caption: Simplified bandwidth model for the 7B shape: a step reads the 13.5 GB base once plus each distinct adapter once. At rank 16, 32 distinct adapters add 19% more bytes.

At rank 64, 32 distinct adapters add 76%, and 64 adapters more than the base itself. High-rank adapters with many distinct tenants per batch erode the batching win; this model ignores KV cache reads and kernel efficiency.
At rank 8 the same 32 adapters add under 10%. Rank is a serving cost, not only a training choice.

blocks.md: SGMV groups rows by adapter and runs all segments in one launch, so a batch can mix adapters while the base matmul stays shared. Its cost grows with the number of distinct adapters and their rank, because each one's weights must be read.

blocks.question: A batch of 64 decode rows is spread across 64 different adapters. According to Punica's roofline analysis, what limits the SGMV kernel?
options: Tensor Core throughput, because there are 64 matmuls
Memory bandwidth, because each row reads its own adapter weights and does little math per byte
PCIe bandwidth, because adapters are always loaded from the CPU
Nothing: the cost is identical to one shared adapter
blocks.explain: With n = s_n the I/O term n h_i h_o grows with the batch, so arithmetic intensity stays about 0.94 FLOP per byte, firmly bandwidth bound. Measured latency rose from 37 to 116 microseconds, versus 37 to 40 for a single shared adapter.

blocks.question: Using the simplified bandwidth model, which change most reduces the extra bytes read per step when 32 distinct adapters share each batch?
options: Raising the batch size to 64
Sorting rows by adapter
Using more prefill tokens per batch
Halving every adapter's rank
blocks.explain: Extra traffic is proportional to (distinct adapters) x rank. Halving the rank halves it. Sorting is required for SGMV to work but does not change how many adapter bytes must be read, and a bigger batch with more tenants can add distinct adapters.

lessons.title: Thousands of adapters: S-LoRA's unified paging and loading

blocks.md: SGMV handles the adapters in a batch. S-LoRA (Sheng et al. 2023) asks the next question: what if there are thousands of adapters and only a few dozen are needed at any moment? Its answer is to keep **all adapters in host (CPU) memory** and copy to the GPU only those used by the currently running batch. The number of adapters is then bounded by host memory, not GPU memory.

Fetching is cheap relative to a decode step. Punica measured loading a LoRA model from host memory over PCIe Gen4 x16 at about 2 ms for the whole adapter (about 50 microseconds per layer), against roughly 30 ms per decode step in its setup, and overlaps the copy with computation. S-LoRA also **prefetches**: while the current batch decodes, it predicts which adapters the waiting queue will need next and loads them early.

The harder problem is GPU memory layout. Recall PagedAttention: the KV cache is split into fixed-size blocks so that requests of different lengths do not fragment memory. Adapters cause the same trouble. They come and go with requests, and their sizes vary with rank. Allocating them contiguously next to a paged KV cache leaves holes.

S-LoRA's observation: in one layer, a request's KV cache has shape $(S, H)$ for $S$ tokens, and a LoRA weight has shape $(R, H)$ for rank $R$. Both are stacks of $H$-sized vectors. **Unified Paging** therefore uses one memory pool whose page is a single $H$-vector. A KV tensor of length $S$ takes $S$ pages and an adapter weight of rank $R$ takes $R$ pages, interleaved anywhere in the pool.

blocks.title: A unified pool of 24 pages (toy, one layer)

scenes.caption: One statically allocated pool fills all GPU memory left after the base weights and activations. Each page holds one H-dimensional vector.
Request r1 arrives using adapter X (toy: one rank-4 weight, 4 pages, tone a) and has 3 tokens of KV cache (3 pages, tone d).
Request r2 uses adapter Y with rank 8, so Y takes 8 pages. Different ranks are just different page counts.
r1 generates 2 more tokens; its KV pages land wherever space is free.
r1 finishes. Its KV pages and adapter X (no longer used) are freed, leaving holes. r2 grows by one page.
r3 arrives with adapter Z (rank 2) and 6 tokens. It fills the holes, non-contiguously. Custom kernels read adapters and KV from scattered pages, so no space is lost to fragmentation.

blocks.md: The pool also makes the tradeoff visible: adapter pages and KV pages compete. Per layer, the S-LoRA paper describes LoRA on the four attention matrices. A rank-16 adapter there is 4 matrices x 2 factors x 16 = 128 pages, the same as 64 tokens of keys plus values. For a 7B model with all seven linear layers adapted at rank 16, the 80 MB adapter equals about 152 tokens of KV cache (0.5 MiB per token). Every adapter resident on the GPU is a few requests' worth of context that cannot be cached.

Two scheduling policies follow. **Adapter clustering** prefers to batch requests that share adapters, leaving more room for KV cache and bigger batches, at some cost to latency and fairness. **Admission control** drops requests that cannot meet the latency target (S-LoRA's early-abort strategy) instead of letting the whole queue miss it. For decode, S-LoRA uses MBGMV, a version of Punica's kernel extended to mixed ranks and non-contiguous pages; for prefill it uses a Triton kernel called MBGMM.

blocks.title: S-LoRA throughput vs number of adapters (Table 3, setting S2)

scenes.caption: Llama-7B with adapters of ranks 8 to 64, one A100 80GB, 5 adapters. vLLM-packed runs one merged vLLM copy per adapter (2.04 req/s); PEFT swaps adapters between batches (0.74).
100 adapters: vLLM-packed runs out of GPU memory (shown as 0). PEFT falls to 0.24 req/s. S-LoRA holds 7.29.
2,000 adapters: S-LoRA still serves 6.71 req/s (6.69 at 1,000). The baselines were out of memory or not run at this scale.

blocks.md: Unified Paging is not magic capacity. Adapter pages and KV pages come from the same pool, so many large adapters active at once shrink the space for KV cache and therefore the batch size. That is why clustering and rank choices still matter.

blocks.question: Why did S-LoRA put adapter weights and KV cache in one paged pool instead of two separate pools?
options: Because both are stacks of H-sized vectors that come and go dynamically, so sharing H-sized pages avoids fragmentation and lets the split between them change with load
Because adapters and KV cache are always the same size
Because the base model weights also need paging
Because PCIe transfers require page-aligned buffers
blocks.explain: A KV tensor is (S, H) and a LoRA weight is (R, H). With pages of one H-vector each, both fit the same allocator, holes left by one can be reused by the other, and the balance shifts automatically between many adapters and long contexts.

blocks.question: A burst of requests touches 40 rarely used adapters at high rank. In S-LoRA's design, what is the most direct cost?
options: The base model must be reloaded
Requests for those adapters must wait for a merge
Adapter pages take space from the KV cache, reducing how many requests fit in a batch, and each adapter must be fetched from host memory
SGMV can no longer batch rows together
blocks.explain: Adapters live in host memory and are fetched on demand into the unified pool. Each active adapter uses pages that the KV cache could have used, so many large ones at once cut the batch size. Nothing is merged, and batching still works.

lessons.title: Multi-LoRA in vLLM and LoRAX, and the cost model

blocks.md: These ideas now ship in open-source servers. In **vLLM** you start the server with LoRA enabled and register adapters; a request then names an adapter as if it were a model, and vLLM batches it with base-model requests and other adapters. Internally, vLLM's LoRA layers go through a component called the Punica wrapper, with Triton kernels named `lora_shrink` and `lora_expand`.

blocks.code:
vllm serve meta-llama/Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct \
    --enable-lora \
    --lora-modules sql-lora=jeeejeee/llama32-3b-text2sql-spider \
    --max-loras 4 --max-lora-rank 16 --max-cpu-loras 32

curl http://localhost:8000/v1/completions \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{"model": "sql-lora", "prompt": "San Francisco is a", "max_tokens": 7}'
blocks.caption: Adapted from the vLLM LoRA docs. The request picks the adapter through the model field.

blocks.md:
The knobs map onto the earlier lessons:
- `max_loras`: how many different adapters can be in one batch (default 1 in current source).
- `max_lora_rank`: the largest rank allowed (default 16 in current source).
- `max_cpu_loras`: how many adapters to keep cached in CPU memory; must be at least `max_loras`.

With `VLLM_ALLOW_RUNTIME_LORA_UPDATING=True`, the server also exposes `/v1/load_lora_adapter` and `/v1/unload_lora_adapter`. The docs warn this carries security risks and belongs only in isolated, trusted environments.

blocks.title: A request for an adapter in a vLLM-style server (simplified)

scenes.caption: An operator registers an adapter at runtime (only with runtime updating enabled).
A request names the adapter in the model field. The scheduler needs it in one of the max_loras GPU slots before the request can join a batch.

add.label: copy A, B into free slot

scenes.caption: The request decodes in a mixed batch with base-model requests and other adapters; tokens stream back.

blocks.md: One implementation detail explains a docs warning. In vLLM's source, each LoRA-wrapped linear layer allocates its adapter buffers up front with shape `(max_loras, 1, max_lora_rank, input_size)` for A and the matching shape for B, and copies a smaller adapter into the top-left corner of a slot. Memory is therefore reserved for `max_loras` adapters at `max_lora_rank`, whatever the real ranks are. The docs advise setting `max_lora_rank` to the largest rank you actually serve.

blocks.title: Reserved LoRA slot memory, 7B shape, max_loras = 4

scenes.caption: Computed from the slot shapes for all seven linear layers of a 32-layer, 4096-wide model in 16-bit: 0.32 GB at rank 16. Simplified: ignores embedding and head adapters.
If every real adapter has rank 16 but you set 256, you reserve 5.12 GB for padding, memory the KV cache could have used. This is the waste S-LoRA's rank-sized pages avoid.

blocks.md: **LoRAX** (LoRA eXchange, from Predibase) is a server built for this use case, forked from Hugging Face's text-generation-inference. Its docs list: dynamic adapter loading per request from the Hugging Face Hub, Predibase or a filesystem; heterogeneous continuous batching that packs requests for different adapters into one batch; adapter exchange scheduling that prefetches and offloads adapters between GPU and CPU; and Punica's SGMV kernel. Launcher flags such as `--max-active-adapters` and `--adapter-cycle-time-s` control how many adapters sit on the GPU and how often they are exchanged. LoRAX can also merge several adapters per request (linear, TIES, DARE).

A cost checklist for a multi-LoRA deployment, all from this course:
1. **Weights**: one base, plus adapter size x number resident (80 MB per rank-16 all-linear adapter for a 7B model).
2. **KV trade**: each resident adapter displaces KV cache (about 152 tokens' worth at that size).
3. **Bandwidth**: each distinct adapter in a batch adds its bytes to every decode step, in proportion to rank.
4. **Cold starts**: a miss costs a host-to-GPU copy (milliseconds) or a disk or network fetch (longer).
5. **Merge** when one adapter dominates; **unmerged** when many are active.

Measure your own adapter mix. Punica and S-LoRA both show that results depend on popularity: identical, skewed (a few hot adapters), or distinct (every request different). Hot adapters can stay resident; the long tail can be loaded on demand.

blocks.question: You serve adapters of rank 8 and 16 with vLLM but set --max-lora-rank 256. What is the main consequence?
options: Requests fail because ranks must match exactly
Adapters are automatically retrained at rank 256
Throughput improves because larger slots are faster
GPU memory is reserved for rank-256 slots, wasting space that the KV cache could use
blocks.explain: vLLM preallocates each of the max_loras slots at max_lora_rank and pads smaller adapters into them. The docs warn that setting it much higher than needed wastes memory and can hurt performance.

blocks.question: Traffic is 95% for one adapter, with a long tail of 300 rarely used adapters. Which design fits best?
options: A multi-LoRA server that keeps the hot adapter resident and loads tail adapters on demand from CPU memory
Merge all 300 into separate model copies
Merge-and-swap on a single GPU for all traffic
Serve only the base model
blocks.explain: The tail is what makes separate or swapped deployments expensive. A multi-LoRA server batches everything over one base, keeps the popular adapter in GPU memory, and fetches rare ones on demand. A dedicated merged copy for the hot adapter can still make sense if its latency is critical.

blocks.question: Which statement about LoRAX matches its documentation?
options: It requires all adapters to be merged before serving
It only supports one adapter per GPU
It batches requests for different adapters together and swaps adapters between GPU and CPU memory
It replaces the base model with a quantized adapter
blocks.explain: LoRAX documents heterogeneous continuous batching (different adapters in one batch) and adapter exchange scheduling (prefetch and offload between GPU and CPU), using Punica's SGMV kernel.
